noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the role of digestive enzymes, including the digestion of starch to glucose by amylase and maltase, the digestion of proteins to amino acids by proteases and the digestion of lipids to fatty acids and glycerol by lipases

primer.text: You know enzymes are biological catalysts and that digestion turns food into absorbable molecules. This lesson names the three enzyme families, the substrates they split and the products released — starch to maltose to glucose, proteins to amino acids, lipids to glycerol and fatty acids — plus where each enzyme is made.

lessons.title: Carbohydrases: Starch to Glucose
lessons.opening: Digestion exists to shrink large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones the blood can carry, and enzymes do most of it chemically. The carbohydrase team handles starch: amylase cuts starch into maltose, and maltase finishes the job by splitting maltose into glucose — the sugar the bloodstream actually absorbs.
keyPoints: Digestion breaks large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones for absorption.
Enzymes are biological catalysts, speeding reactions without being consumed.
Carbohydrases break carbohydrates into simple sugars such as glucose.
Amylase splits starch into maltose and is made in the salivary glands and pancreas.
Maltase, made in the small intestine, converts maltose into glucose.
Mechanical digestion by chewing and churning enlarges the surface enzymes work on.

low.restatement: Amylase halves starch to maltose; maltase finishes maltose to glucose.
low.analogy: A two-stage scissors line trimming a ribbon to confetti.
low.examPointer: Give substrate and product for each enzyme — both names earn marks.

medium.restatement: Where an enzyme is made and where it acts can differ: salivary amylase dies in the stomach acid, while pancreatic amylase works on arrival in the intestine.
medium.analogy: A courier whose parcel is destroyed in one district but delivered safely in another.
medium.examPointer: Know the production sites and the fate of salivary amylase in the stomach.

check.stem: What is the purpose of digestion overall?

options.text: To break large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones the blood can absorb
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: To store food for later use
options.explanation: Storage is not digestion's purpose.

options.text: To heat food to enzyme temperature
options.explanation: Warmth helps but is not the purpose.

options.text: To remove water from food
options.explanation: Water absorption happens, but digestion's aim is molecular.

check.stem: Which enzyme breaks starch into maltose?

options.text: Amylase
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Maltase
options.explanation: Maltase acts on maltose, finishing the job to glucose.

options.text: Pepsin
options.explanation: Pepsin is a protease acting on protein.

options.text: Lipase
options.explanation: Lipase splits lipids.

check.stem: Where is maltase made and where does it act?

options.text: Made and acting in the small intestine
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Made in the salivary glands, acting there
options.explanation: Salivary glands make amylase.

options.text: Made in the stomach, acting in the intestine
options.explanation: The stomach makes protease, not maltase.

options.text: Made by the pancreas alone
options.explanation: The pancreas produces amylase, not maltase.

check.stem: Why is salivary amylase denatured in the stomach?

options.text: Stomach acid is far below the pH amylase works at
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The stomach is too cold for enzymes
options.explanation: Temperature is not the stated cause.

options.text: Maltase destroys amylase on contact
options.explanation: Enzymes do not destroy one another.

options.text: Starch is absent in the stomach
options.explanation: Starch arrives with the food; the enzyme is what fails.

check.stem: Why does mechanical digestion help chemical digestion?

options.text: Breaking food into smaller pieces increases the surface area enzymes can work on
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It denatures the enzymes first
options.explanation: Churning prepares food, not enzymes.

options.text: It replaces the need for enzymes
options.explanation: Both act together.

options.text: It raises the pH of the food
options.explanation: Mechanical action changes no pH.

check.stem: State the product of amylase acting on starch.
check.modelAnswer: Amylase breaks starch down into maltose.

check.stem: Name the enzyme that converts maltose into glucose.
check.modelAnswer: Maltase converts maltose into glucose in the small intestine.

check.stem: Explain why the small intestine produces a small amount of amylase itself.
check.modelAnswer: Because salivary amylase is denatured by stomach acid before much starch is split, the intestine tops up the supply so starch digestion can still finish there, alongside maltase completing maltose to glucose.

check.stem: A cracker held in the mouth turns sweet. Explain using the carbohydrase pathway.
check.modelAnswer: Salivary amylase in the saliva splits the cracker's starch into maltose, and some maltase activity finishes it toward glucose; those sugars taste sweet, demonstrating the first stage of carbohydrate digestion beginning in the mouth.

lessons.title: Proteases and Lipases
lessons.opening: The protease line starts with pepsin in the stomach, splitting proteins into shorter polypeptide chains, and finishes with pancreatic and intestinal proteases releasing amino acids. Alongside, lipases from the pancreas split lipids into glycerol and fatty acids in the small intestine — with bile's emulsification already having enlarged the surface they attack.
keyPoints: Proteases break proteins down into amino acids.
Pepsin, made in the stomach, cuts proteins into shorter polypeptide chains.
Pancreatic and intestinal proteases finish the chains into amino acids.
Lipases split lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.
Lipase comes from the pancreas, arriving in the small intestine by secretion.
The pancreas is an accessory organ: food never passes through it.

low.restatement: Pepsin starts protein work; other proteases finish; lipase splits fats.
low.analogy: A demolition crew: first pass breaks the frame, second pass clears the bricks.
low.examPointer: Quote the products exactly — amino acids; glycerol and fatty acids.

medium.restatement: Each protease works where its pH suits it: pepsin in acid, the later proteases in alkaline conditions.
medium.analogy: Two specialists on shift at different hours.
medium.examPointer: Remember the pancreas makes enzymes but receives no food — a favourite trick question.

check.stem: What do proteases produce from proteins?

options.text: Amino acids
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Glucose
options.explanation: Glucose comes from carbohydrate digestion.

options.text: Glycerol and fatty acids
options.explanation: Those are lipase's products.

options.text: Maltose
options.explanation: Maltose is an intermediate of starch digestion.

check.stem: Where is pepsin made, and on what does it act?

options.text: In the stomach, breaking proteins into shorter polypeptide chains
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: In the pancreas, on lipids
options.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes handle later stages.

options.text: In the intestine, on starch
options.explanation: Intestinal enzymes act on several substrates, but pepsin is stomach-made.

options.text: In the liver, on fats
options.explanation: The liver makes bile, not pepsin.

options.text: Glycerol and fatty acids
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Amino acids
options.explanation: Protease products.

options.text: Glucose and oxygen
options.explanation: Photosynthesis products.

options.text: Maltose and starch
options.explanation: Starch-digestion intermediates.

check.stem: Which organ produces lipase and where is it secreted to?

options.text: The pancreas produces it, and it is secreted into the small intestine
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The stomach produces it, acting there
options.explanation: The stomach makes pepsin.

options.text: The liver produces it, stored in the gall bladder
options.explanation: The liver makes bile.

options.text: The salivary glands produce it
options.explanation: They make amylase.

check.stem: Why is the pancreas called an accessory organ?

options.text: Food never passes through it, yet it supplies digestive enzymes and insulin
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because it is the smallest digestive organ
options.explanation: Size is not the criterion.

options.text: Because it only works during fasting
options.explanation: It secretes when chyme arrives.

options.text: Because it absorbs the digested products
options.explanation: Absorption is the intestine's role.

check.stem: Name the enzyme made in the stomach that digests protein.
check.modelAnswer: Pepsin is made in the stomach and breaks down proteins.

check.stem: State the end products of protein digestion.
check.modelAnswer: Protein digestion ends with amino acids, released by the combined proteases.

check.stem: Explain why proteins need two stages of protease digestion.
check.modelAnswer: Because whole proteins are far too large to absorb in one step; pepsin first shortens them into polypeptide chains, and the pancreatic and intestinal proteases then finish the chains into amino acids small enough to pass into the blood.

check.stem: Bile has emulsified a fatty meal. Describe the lipase step that follows.
check.modelAnswer: With the fat now spread into tiny droplets, pancreatic lipase secreted into the small intestine attacks the much larger surface, chemically splitting the lipid molecules into glycerol and fatty acids for absorption.

glossary.definition: An enzyme family that breaks carbohydrates into simple sugars such as glucose.
An enzyme that digests protein, ending in amino acids.
The enzyme that splits lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.
